cultivar: Qingxin Damou (Qing Xin Da Mou) in Hsinchu and Miaoli; Qingxin oolong for the lighter 'white-tip' versions from Pinglin and Shiding
processing: Hand-picked bud-and-two-leaf shoots bitten by the tea green leafhopper, withered and oxidised heavily (figures run from about 60% up to 85%), pan-fired, then wrapped in damp cloth to rest and soften before rolling (the hui ruan step) and dried at low heat; usually no real roast, though some lots get a finishing bake, and no pesticides because the insects are needed.
harvest_season: One main harvest in early summer, around the Grain in Ear solar term in June, when leafhopper activity peaks; small autumn pickings exist but the June tea is what the name means.
appearance_dry: Loose, twisted leaves in five colours, white fuzzy buds with green, yellow, red and brown leaf, soft and light in the hand.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber-orange, like a light honey.
appearance_wet: Small, soft leaves with brown-red edges and pale buds, bitten and puckered at the margins.
taste_profile: Honey, ripe peach and muscat grape with a silky, almost fizzy sweetness and no astringency; cooler brewing keeps it soft.

brewing.notes: Cooler than other oolongs, around 85 °C, with the gaiwan filled generously because the leaf is light and bulky; boiling water flattens it and brings out sourness. Also Western-style at 3 g per cup, and a superb cold brew.

vintage_note: Sold by summer harvest year and above all by competition grade: Hsinchu County holds its judged competition in Beipu or Emei in June and July, Miaoli County holds one in July, and both also run a winter round in November or December. Graded lots go out in small sealed packs at prices that climb steeply with the grade and the share of white buds. Garden tea is sold as the June harvest of the current year; it keeps two or three years sealed and is not usually aged. Lighter 'white-tip oolong' from Pinglin and Shiding is a cheaper cousin made from Qing Xin oolong.
description:
Oriental Beauty is the heavily oxidised, white-tipped oolong of the Hakka hill country of Hsinchu and Miaoli, and the tea that made leafhopper damage a virtue. The tea green leafhopper feeds on the young shoots in early summer, the bush responds by producing the compounds that smell of honey and ripe fruit, and the farmers of Emei, Beipu, Toufen and Sanwan turn that damaged leaf into one of the most expensive teas in Taiwan. Locals call it Peng Feng Cha, 'braggart's tea', after the story of the farmer nobody believed when he said how much he had sold it for; the English name is said to come from a European royal, which is a legend.

It is picked once a year in the way that matters, around the Grain in Ear solar term in June, by hand, as a bud and two leaves from unsprayed gardens of the Qing Xin Da Mou cultivar. The leaf is withered and heavily oxidised, with figures running from about 60 percent up to 85, pan-fired, then wrapped in damp cloth to rest and soften before being rolled and dried at low heat. Most lots get no real roast, though a finishing bake on some deepens the liquor. The finished leaf shows five colours, white buds and green, yellow, red and brown leaf, which is where the name 'five-colour tea' comes from.

The cup is honey, ripe peach and muscat grape with a silky, almost fizzy sweetness and no astringency at all. Brew it cooler than other oolongs, around 85 degrees, with the gaiwan filled generously because the leaf is light and bulky; boiling water flattens it and brings out a sourness. It gives five or six steeps gongfu-style, works Western-style at three grams per cup, and cold-brews into something close to a dessert wine.

It is sold by summer harvest year and, above all, by competition grade: Hsinchu and Miaoli counties hold judged competitions after the summer harvest and again in winter, and graded lots go out in small sealed packs at prices that climb steeply with the grade and the proportion of white buds. The lighter 'white-tip oolong' of Pinglin and Shiding is made from Qing Xin oolong and is a cheaper cousin, and a lot of 'Oriental Beauty' from Thailand, Vietnam and mainland China is sold without saying so. Honey in the empty cup and bitten, puckered leaf edges are the tell.

It keeps two or three years sealed and is not usually aged. Serve it with pastry or after a meal; it is the oolong to convert people who think they only like black tea.
sources_note: Competition grade names follow the general Taiwanese farmers' association scheme; the exact tier list for the Emei and Beipu competitions should be checked. The 'named by a European queen' story is flagged as legend.
history:
This tea goes back to the late nineteenth century, when Taiwan first exported oolong through merchants like John Dodd at Tamsui, in the Hakka hills of northwestern Taiwan. Lots were sent to Dadaocheng for a final bake and sorting in the fan-zhuang workshops before shipping, which gave the old name Fan Zhuang oolong, still used in Miaoli.

Farmers named it after the pest. The Taiwanese names all point at the insect, and as prices rose the bragging name took over: Peng Feng, 'braggart's tea', from the usual story of the Beipu farmer whose neighbours would not believe what a merchant had paid for his bitten leaf.

The name Oriental Beauty is a matter of legend. One story has Queen Victoria naming it, another places it around 1960 with Elizabeth II after a prize at a food fair in Britain, and neither has evidence behind it; the Victoria version does not fit the dates. In 1983 Miaoli's tea was called Fu Shou tea, a name given by Vice President Hsieh Tung-min, before reverting.

The names now divide the map: Peng Feng in Beipu, Oriental Beauty in Emei, Fan Zhuang in Toufen and Sanwan. Hsinchu and Miaoli counties hold judged competitions in summer and again in winter, and the method has inspired bug-bitten Dong Ding and east-coast black teas.
